maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, may I say just a word about this, because I think it is one of the most important measures contemplated for this session. At the present time the cost of living has reached an alltime high. Though there was a slight reduction a month ago, the latest report from the bureau of statistics indicates that the cost of living has now reached the highest figure in our history.
It seems to me the government needs to consider this because of the effect it is having on all the people of Canada. If we look at the price index for 1945, when the war ended, and compare the figures with the present index, we find an increase that is phenomenal. The cost of living index in August, 1945, stood at 119-6. It has now risen to 159-6. That is a tremendous increase since the removal of controls; and the effect, of course, is really disastrous on people with small and fixed incomes, such as veterans and other pensioners, or people whose wages or salary have not gone up to any extent. It seems to me this is a matter with which the house should grapple this session. I have noticed that in the United States, for example, where the increase has been greater than here and the cost of living figure is higher, in his message to congress President Truman indicated the necessity of doing something about the restoration of controls if the cost of living did not come down. And I would

Transitional Measures Act say the government should bear in mind the lesson of the United States election, because President Truman campaigned up and down that country on issues of the sort the C.C.F. has been endeavouring to bring to this house for the past several years.
One of them, of course, is this matter of the increased cost of living. Actually what has happened is that today a dollar is worth only seventy-five cents as compared with the end of the war, in the basic commodities that it will buy. Think of the effect of this upon old age pensioners, for example. While there was a slight increase of $5 a month some eighteen months or two years ago, this means that the $30 they get today will buy only as much as $22.50 would buy in 1945, only three and a half years ago. And this increased cost of living, coming at the same time as the enormous increases in profits of some of our corporations are being published, is bound to provoke a great deal of discussion among those who know the real facts. All during the war our people were encouraged to buy victory bonds, to invest in war savings certificates, and all the rest of it. They were encouraged to save every dollar. At that time a dollar would buy a dollar's worth of goods; today it will buy only seventy-five cents' worth. It seems to me that is a very serious matter for all concerned, and particularly for those who made the savings several years ago.
I have other figures here. Everyone knows the manner in which the costs of production on the farm have gone up. It is said that the cost of living in urban areas has risen more sharply than on the farms, but as a matter of fact the figures do not bear out that statement. The index of farm living costs has risen by 38 per cent since 1945, compared with a 33 per cent increase in the general cost of living. Nor can it be said that this is due to the cash income of the farmer. The total cash income from the sale of farm products went up 17 per cent from 1945 to 1947. When you turn to the distributor, you find the profits of the largest food companies have risen by 47 per cent.
Sometimes it is said that wages are responsible for the rise in the cost of living. Weekly wages and salaries, for example, in one of our best paid industries, iron and steel, went up by nine per cent, while profits in that industry have risen by 66 per cent; in pulp and paper, wages are up 23 per cent and profits are up 247 per cent. I could continue the examination of the manner in which the great mass of people are being penalized by the tremendous rise in the cost of living. Consequently, Mr. Speaker, I think this is a matter that the house cannot pass over lightly.
[Mr. Caldwell. 1

I am glad to see that the government intends to ask parliament to continue certain powers which parliament conferred upon it in order to cope with this situation. But something more is necessary than pious hopes and asking for the continuance of power, if our people are to be rescued from this tremendous increase in costs which are adversely affecting all of them, with the exception of those who benefit from the increased returns in certain classes of industry and business. I do not want to pursue this, Mr. Speaker. I have emphasized the increased cost of living. I believe the government intends to continue rent controls under this authority; that is a good thing as far as it goes.
After the removal of certain aspects of rent controls made a short time ago, I was told of cases where increases were made, particularly in the newer buildings, which put them beyond the reach of people with average incomes. If these controls were removed altogether the shortage of houses would cause rents and values to shoot sky-high. When we come to the bill itself, these are matters that should receive very thorough consideration. I just wanted to say I am glad the government is going ahead with this resolution. I hope it will reconsider its whole position with regard to controls and subsidies. As a matter of fact, I think subsidies of some types are necessary and fully warranted at this time.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is he aware of the fact that the first reduction in the cost of living in the United States was made in meat by that octopus, the meat packers and abattoirs, which reduction was later followed by the retail merchants? This octopus, about which our friends are so glib, set the example for the reduction in the cost of living. That is private enterprise.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am very glad indeed to find that we have at least one defender of the organizations which he himself describes as a great octopus.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I was using the hon. member's words. He so described it. I used those words so that he would recognize it.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Well, I recognize an octopus when I see it.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Where are you looking-over there?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I was not looking at the member for Calgary West when I said that. What I was going to say, Mr. Speaker, when

I was interrupted a few minutes ago, was that perhaps what the hon. member says is partly true.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I ask
hon. members not to interrupt. They will please observe the rules of the house. It is not in order to interrupt any member who has the floor. I am sure hon. members will co-operate with the Speaker in this regard.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: What I was going to say is that if it is true, and I believe it may be, that the packing interests in the United States did begin the reduction in the price of meat, that only underlines the fact that for months and even years before that reduction was made they were reaping enormous profits. So far as our own meat-packing industry is concerned, a year ago last Christmas, when the government removed certain controls, the packers had quite a large backlog of meat and other commodities. This enabled them to reap a very good harvest at that time and should enable them to make a reduction in the price of meat in this country.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: And butter.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Probably butter, but I am not conversant with that now; a year ago it was true.
I do not propose to say any more at this stage. I think that more than rent control is necessary, and the government should consider, either by subsidy or by the exercise of powers conferred upon it by parliament, ways and means of endeavouring to bring down the cost of living within reasonable bounds.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion which has been presented simply calls for the resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war.
This is a very different basis from that of the resolution we dealt with this afternoon. In that case, we knew the principle involved, but in this case we certainly have not the information which would enable us to deal with the resolution. I believe the house should have a full explanation from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) as to what emergency regulations it is intended to continue and what the effect will be, before the house is called upon to vote on this resolution.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I rise to a point of order. Is the minister going to close the debate? He moved the motion; that constituted his first speech. When he speaks the second time, he closes the debate.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words on this resolution.
Transitional Measures Act In the first place, the minister is asking for something for which he should not be asking. Justice and law are not synonymous terms. The enforcement of the law is the responsibility of the provincial attorneys general, and they turn it off on the municipal police. There is no way of enforcing these laws. I forget how many orders in council were passed during the war, but I think it was something like 180,000. The war is now over. In the old country complaints have been made about the same thing. The other day in the British House of Commons the attorney general, Sir Hartley Shawcross, was complaining about the high cost of litigation today. Mr. Churchill supported him. Since the war closed 25,000 orders in council there have been passed. Nobody knows the law. Only five of these orders in council have been before the courts. Rules and regulations have been made from them which have the force of statutes. Complaints were made the other day in the British House of Commons about the high cost of litigation. I have been complaining here about the same thing for a long time. Nobody knows the cost of litigation today. Sir Hartley spoke on this matter at Lincoln's Inn, and Mr. Churchill referred to it in a radio speech.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) is asking for something that should not be asked for, now that the war is over. In England nobody knows what the law is until it is interpreted by the privy council. Only five of these orders in council, and the rules and regulations which have the force of a statute, have come before the law courts. That should not be. As I say, the enforcement of these orders in council rests with the municipal police force, and they get nothing for it. In New South Wales the federal government of Australia gives Sydney $2,500,000 as a subvention to the city police to enforce the federal law. What is the result? We have all these violations. Only five of these orders in council have ever come before the Supreme Court of Canada and 20,000 of them altogether have been passed since the war; and the rules and regulations made under those orders in council have the force of statutes. As I say, law and justice are not synonymous terms. In 1491 B.C. Moses gave us the ten commandments. I would call to the attention of the house and the government the simplicity of those commandments compared to the laws that must be enforced by the courts today. Law reform is badly needed in this country. We have no law reform at all.
Is this law reform, to impose these orders in council which were passed during the war for emergency purposes? I say no; it is not law reform at all. Who is to enforce these orders in council? Enforcement is on the municipal police, and they do not get a cent

Transitional Measures Act for it. I can tell hon. members this. The ten commandments are simplicity itself, and everybody understands them. Not so these orders in council which are proposed now, long after the war is over.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, we should have some statement from the government regarding these matters, because only five of these orders in council have ever been interpreted by the Supreme Court of Canada. Yet they are imposed on all the citizens of this country, although they may not be legal. Nobody knows whether they are legal or not until they are interpreted by the privy council. Even my hon. friends to my left just recently appealed to the privy council with regard to certain legislation. If it is legal to impose these orders in council years after the war is over, I fail to see it. Nobody knows what the law is. Osgoode Hall cannot tell you what the law is. There is no finality to it on an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. The judges and magistrates are imposing these orders in council on the poor working classes of this country, and I say that the principle of it is all wrong. The municipal police get nothing for the enforcement of these orders in council, and the federal government does not itself enforce federal laws. Nobody knows what the law is until it is interpreted. Only five of them have come before the privy council.
What I am complaining about is the high cost of litigation today. The result is that everybody settles his case. Everyone must settle his case owing to the high cost of litigation. The other day in England Mr. Churchill was complaining about it, but no one in this house has done so except myself; I have been complaining for three or four years and asking for law reform. We have never had any law reform under any Minister of Justice. From Moses down to the present Minister of Justice is a long route. If this is the law reform he proposes, I am opposed to it. I can tell him that the enforcement of laws is on the provincial attorney general and he turns it over to the municipal police.
My friends on my left are no doubt extremely eager. My friend the whip down there is not a lawyer, but he knows something about law. The magistrates are convicting people illegally, as are county court judges. This matter came up in the British House of Commons, and the law was quoted to them over there, and what is being done even in this country. In England many of these things have been complained about, and it is not law reform at all. There is no law reform. As I say, the magistrates are convicting people on orders in council which are absolutely illegal. There has been no law

reform that I can see. I am complaining today not only about the extension of this act but about the rules and regulations, passed under the act, which have the force of statutes. If you go to any lawyer, he cannot tell you what the law is with regard to these matters.
In England an effort was made to upset some of these orders in council, and only one county court judge questioned the law. What is being proposed here by this resolution is to extend these orders in council. The resolution says that it is expedient to do so. I say it is not expedient, years after the war, to impose on the people all these rules and regulations, which have the force of statutes and which have never been passed by this house. They are absolutely illegal. I could name some of them. I referred the other day to an adjourned debate in the British house in which reference was made to the fact that in a town called Stevenage in England all the houses were torn down. An appeal was taken to the law courts. Only one magistrate questioned the proceedings. He expressed the opinion that nothing like it had been done since the time of Ahab, who was a king of Samaria, when he took Naboth's vineyard. A county court judge questioned the law, and he was supported in the British House of Commons accordingly. He quoted the law. Naboth had a vineyard. It was taken away from him. Wh can find all about that in the second book of Kings.
The next thing that came up was paper money. The government in the old country passed another act and Shawcross, the attorney general of England, took it up. Mr. Churchill complained about the high cost of litigation. He said there were only five orders in council that came before the courts. There were 25,000 orders in council passed.
Is it any wonder that the poor people back home are disgusted? I see them lined up in the police court waiting to pay their fines because they had not paid $2.50 for a radio licence. They were charged $5 and costs by the magistrate. It is all illegal. They are convicted because of the actions of that mischievous institution, the C.B.C. They summoned 7,000 citizens in our city. They have a special magistrate. The magistrates do not know the law. They know it in England. What did they say in England? Mr. Churchill referred to it. First they go to the borough magistrate; then to the county court judge.
The government is introducing a measure dealing with emergency powers to go into patent law, trade-mark law and all these things. The other day in England Mr. Churchill referred to the high cost of litigation. Everybody understands the ten comnvtr. Church.]

mandments, but who can understand the voluminous judgments that we are getting from the Supreme Court of Canada and the other courts in Osgoode Hall? Everybody can understand the simplicity of the ten commandments, but who can understand some of the judgments which are contained in the law reports which the lawyers are getting in this country today? Is that law reform? It is no wonder the people in Toronto and in constituencies throughout the country are complaining about the high cost of litigation. People are being haled before the magistrates, and some of them have no money. If that is the kind of law reform we are facing here tonight all I can say is that I am opposed to it.
Another thing is the 25,000 orders in council. Mr. Churchill complained about the same thing in England the other day. Take the law of income tax under which people are summoned and all that kind of thing. In England the application came before the borough body. I forget what they call it now. My memory is not as good as it was. In England under the exchequer court act they are required to hear and determine the application. But what did they do? This matter came before the borough magistrate and then the special commissioner of income tax. Then it went to the high court of justice, to the court of appeal and all that kind of thing. In England the courts are required to hear the application under an express clause of the exchequer court's proviso. They must hear and determine the merits of the application. A learned English lawyer, P. St. George Kirke, is my authority in this regard.
Then we have trade-marks and paper money. We are meeting here and we are prepared to pass all these things seriatim. I am going to oppose it. We must have constitutional reform, parliamentary reform, cabinet reform and most of all law reform. We have never had any law reform since I have been a member of the house. I have been a member for a long time. I am opposed to the whole program of the attorney general. I had hoped that that portfolio would go to Ontario, because Sir Wilfrid Laurier, when he was elected away back in 1896, appointed David Mills as Minister of Justice from Ontario. Quebec has had a Minister of Justice and solicitor general as head of the law of this country. I had hoped that Ontario would be favoured.
There is no emergency. The resolution says "It is expedient." Is it expedient to fine people as they have been fined in Ontario and in other provinces? They have fined
7,000	people in my city. The magistrates have fined them $5 and costs for not having a radio licence. The return I received three
Transitional Measures Act years ago showed that the city of Ottawa and the city of Hull across the river had not one single case in the courts, but 7,000 people were summoned before the magistrates in my city. The magistrate says, "$5 and costs, you can pay it or not." If that is law reform, five years after Germany collapsed, I say, God help the country, God help the people who have to pay for it.
You can understand the ten commandments, but can anybody understand the voluminous law reports which we are getting from Osgoode Hall and from many other courts? They wear new robes of office. They have new robes of ermine and gold. Where did they get authority for this? Is that law reform? They are dressed in all the colours of the rainbow. It is all vanity and conceit. Vanity of vanities, said the preacher, all is vanity. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) may smile. I have never had the privilege of meeting him. They say that he is not a bad fellow personally. Is that the law reform we are looking for? I noticed a lot of-people from the constituency of the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) in the courts the other day. I asked, "What are you doing here?" They said, "We are down here to pay $5." They call that law reform.
My hon. friends to my left say that they are the same as the Labour government in England. Well, if they are they do not believe in law reform. Who knows the law today? No lawyer can tell us what the law is. They do not know the law. The magistrates' courts are the first courts. Then we have the county court judges' courts. Members from the county court bench come to Toronto and fine the people there. They should know something about these orders in council and the rules and regulations which are actually illegal. I have never seen them. The Minister of Justice has never seen them. That applies to the income tax law and to every statute which has been passed. If that is law reform, then God help the people of this country, because there is no such thing as law reform.
I asked the Minister of Justice last session to appoint a legal committee to go into this matter. He said he would consider it. He has now appointed another commission. It seems to me that we shall become a nation of professors. These are not professors at law. But the fact is that we are becoming a nation of professors. I count that day lost when I do not read about some order in council passed appointing two professors, plus somebody else, to some job. We are nothing but a nation of professors-professor this and professor that. There are very few professors I know of in the universities now who want to hold their jobs; they would rather have

Transitional Measures Act these jobs. In the Annapolis valley they used to say that an apple a day kept the doctor away; but we know that a professor a day will not keep the tax collector away, especially when he is enforcing some of these famous orders in council which have been placed on the statute books.
Fortunately in the mother country they have closed off much of this. I can tell you this, that in my own constituency in Toronto many youths have been sent to jail because of these orders in council-and some women, too, who did not have the money to pay the fines imposed for infractions of some of these emergency regulations. They go to prison when they have not the money to pay the fines.
In that connection, a farm on Yonge Street, Toronto, was taken over for men, and another for women at Concord. That was taken away illegally from the city. Is that law reform? I call this to the attention of the government.
In conclusion let me say this. If that is the kind of justice and law reform the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) has in mind, then I repeat that law and justice are not synonymous terms, although some people think they are.
Let us compare these emergency regulations with what has been done in England. Let us consider, too, the high cost of litigation today. Let us look at the divorce cases, which have become such a nuisance to high court judges that they want to get rid of them and place them before the county court judges.
Here we have involved magistrates and county court judges, and other judicial officials-and I have great respect for them all. They are enforcing fines and imprisonment as a result of regulations which never have passed the House of Commons. Yet I have not heard one of those regulations questioned. They say it is expedient, when in fact it is not expedient at all to provide for the continuance of certain orders and regulations.
These regulations were never necessary. They were issued by someone in this building, or someone in Ottawa. People are being fined as a result of these rules and regulations made by the governor in council. There are so many of them that no one knows what the law is. Only five of them have ever come before the supreme court, and it would take about two thousand years to interpret them. How long it would take to interpret 200,000, I do not know.
I have risen to speak for the protection of the Minister of Justice, and to ask him to do what his predecessor said he would do, namely, to have a legal committee. A legal committee should consider these legal bills.
I do not wish to take up further the time of the house. The minister has been in the
house only a few days, and I have no desire to embarrass him or to say anything unkind to him. But I do call his attention to the high cost of litigation today in this country; no one can afford it. The result is that people are paying fines on orders issued by departmental officials about which lawyers and judges do not know. The lawyers and judges do not know the law in this connection. No one knows it, and it is interpreted by the privy council. My hon. friends to the left have had it before the privy council.
I believe it would be well if we had a legal committee to consider all these bills, and these rules and regulations. Then we could have some means of saving people from paying these fines, when they should not pay them.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
If I may continue the
explanation, the Department of Trade and
Transitional Measures Act Commerce administers three controls which it is proposed to continue. The first is steel control, the second timber control, and the third priorities control. Of these, the most necessary is steel control. As hon. members know, Canada's production of steel has been and continues to be greatly short of Canada's requirements. We have been importing roughly 30 per cent of all the steel that is used, and those imports have been obtained with a great deal of difficulty. By the control of steel it is possible to utilize Canada's production of basic steel to the full capacity of our finishing works. At the present time we are moving surplus primary steel, or semi-finished steel, from the Algoma Steel Company to the finishing plants at Hamilton, to the amount of about 18,000 tons per month. We are also moving semi-finished steel from the Dominion Steel and Coal Company at Sydney to Hamilton, to the extent of about
10.000	tons per month. That 28,000 tons of steel, which cannot be finished at Algoma or at Sydney, would ordinarily go for export and be finished in other countries. That was the pre-war history of the surpluses of those two plants. By moving that steel to Hamilton
28.000	tons per month of additional basic steel are turned into finished products.
The department also has the responsibility of dividing the limited tonnage of pig iron so that the foundries of the country can be kept in operation. We also have the responsibility of allocating scrap which is in very short supply, and which today comes largely from foreign countries. To end steel control abruptly at this time would, I am sure, reduce the production of finished steel from Canadian plants and Canadian foundries by as much as 20 per cent. Price control is maintained, as I think it should be, where an acute shortage exists. All steel is handled under rigid price control. I think that the industry as a whole welcomes control since it assures to each his fair share of Canadian production. I know of no demand that the control be ended; I know there is a general desire that it be continued, and I consider it definitely in the best interests of Canadian industry that it should continue for a further period.
The importance of timber control is less apparent. Only certain grades of timber are in short supply, but on the west coast particularly there is an active demand for the high grades of timber, the clears. These can be sold to the full capacity of the cut. There is a surplus of low grades. Low grades are not selling nearly as well as clears, particularly in export markets. Without control Canada would be stripped of its supply of clear lumber from the west coast. It is believed to be in the interests of Canadian industry that

Transitional Measures Act this control be continued for a certain period. It is being relaxed as opportunity offers, and it may probably be removed before many months go by, but at the moment it is considered necessary.

No, it operates across Canada, but its importance is greater on the west coast on account of the export demand for clear timber.
The priorities control is used almost exclusively in connection with low-cost housing. Supplies for low-cost housing are not yet easily obtainable. Large-scale buyers for larger projects have a definite advantage in bidding for these materials. It is felt that without priorities control the building of low-cost housing would be severely handicapped. It is likely that the duration of that control may not extend beyond many months, but today for materials such as my hon. friend opposite mentions so frequently, nails and products of that kind, it does assure more equitable distribution than would be possible if we did not have a priorities control.

speechtext: I may say I am not familiar with the factors that may have led to the defeat of the government today in Nicolet-Yamaska, but I can tell the government members that we are discussing in this resolution tonight one of the factors that has led to loss after loss sustained by the government since the general election of 1945.

speechtext:
My hon. friends opposite
pounded their desks a great deal a few days

ago when a number of new members were brought in, but I remind the government, and the rank and file of those opposite, that since 1945 six seats that went Liberal on June 11, 1945, have since been lost. The government has picked up only two new seats. In other words, it has sustained a net loss of four seats since the general election. To complete the picture, my hon. friends to the right have had a net gain of two. We in this group have had a net gain of three. The Social Credit group has had a net gain of one. The Cartier seat was formerly held by a Labour-Progressive. The seat of Laval-Two Mountains was formerly held by an Independent. They are the only two seats the government has picked up in the last four years.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, this is not something for my hon. friends to the right to gloat about tonight. Neither is it something to justify my hon. friends opposite in making smart replies; rather it presents them with something they should think over very seriously.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: They will.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am satisfied there are
many members opposite who know just as well as I do that one of the main reasons the government has been losing ground since 1945 has been the way in which it has bungled its policies having to do with the cost of living.
Several things have been turning the people of this country against the government they elected, though by a minority vote, in 1945: its failure to do anything substantial or adequate in regard to housing; its failure to make proper moves in matters of social security, including a proper old age pension and health insurance; its failure to keep down the cost of living. In fact, if you want to point your finger at one fundamental cause of the loss of ground by this government, it is right here in this question of the high cost of living. In addition to all the other fears and dis-illusionments the Canadian people are experiencing today, it is most disturbing to see the way the value of the dollar has shrunk, the plight of our old age pensioners, our superannuated civil servants, our veterans on burnt-out pensions, and others, and also the way in which the increased wages and incomes in the pockets of our people have become worth less because of the rise in the cost of living.
This is a subject, Mr. Speaker, with which, as hon. members of this house know, we are familiar, and as to which we could go on and on. But I am going to stop, for the reason that I think perhaps I may make my case

stronger if I put it as I have, and say to the government that unless they wake up while there is yet time this continuing rise in the cost of living-and it is still going up despite the fact that there was a slight recession in the report before the last one-will result in their being turned out of office when the election is called. I submit that for the wellbeing of the Canadian people they should, while there is yet time, make a turn in the direction they have been traveling and do something about this continually rising cost of living. In this measure now before us there is a chance for the government to amend and revise the bill which is to be based upon this resolution, and go in the direction of restoring price controls. Conditions today demand a determined effort to bring down the cost of living and improve the standard of living of our Canadian people; failure to do this will not be tolerated.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I realize that when we get into committee stage we will be in a much better position to look for answers to pertinent questions in regard to this resolution, but I ask the indulgence of the house while I make one or two general observations. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that these observations will not be of the kind to which I have just listened. Just why at this stage any honourable and intelligent member of this chamber should get up and discuss whether or not the government has the confidence of the people is beyond my comprehension. Surely anyone and everyone must know what is going on in Canada at the moment. The confidence of the people is slipping away from the present administration faster and faster all the time; and that does not need to be brought to the attention of this honourable assembly, using this as a vehicle to bring it to the attention of the fourth estate in order that they may spread the word across Canada. Why, already this fourth estate, to which I seldom have the privilege of speaking, have told the people from Vancouver to Halifax what is transpiring; and what they say tomorrow morning no doubt will not only emphasize but underline in every paragraph what they have been saying previously, so that when the time comes the people will arouse themselves and put in an administration a little more to their liking than the one we have had since 1945.
My purpose in rising, Mr. Speaker, is to mention two or three matters of a general nature on which the government might cogitate until such time as we get into committee of the whole. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), who has been a kind of omnibus minister, who has had his finger in almost every pie it has been my privilege to see cut into during the last decade, must
Transitional Measures Act know something about what he is going to do in connection with this resolution, because he has been part and parcel of its subject matter. Not only that; he has been the boss. What he said went, and probably that is still the case. Every job needs a boss. Just how efficient and capable that boss may be, or how he may be regarded by those under his control, is another matter. I remember that in my younger days I told my boss I thought a certain thing might have been done in a certain way. I remember so well that he pointed to his white shirt and said, "Why do 1 wear a white shirt? Just to show you young people who is boss around here."
The day of the Minister of Trade and Commerce wearing a white shirt to show who is boss around here has gone by, and from here on I suggest that he should be cautious. At the same time, as I said before, in order that members of the government may have something to cogitate about, I want to mention one or two matters of moment. May I preface my remarks by making a general observation, expressing my own opinion, not something I read in some journal, though perhaps the opinion more or less settled itself upon me because I read the journals now and then.
I am of opinion that general commodity prices the world over and particularly on the North American continent are starting to go down. They are following the curve that obtained in 1921-22, just after the first war, when in 1922 prices slipped so badly that they were only about one-third the prices in 1920. If anyone examines commodity prices today he will see that the same course is being followed, in almost the same period of time to the month from cessation of hostilities.
The disaster of 1921-22, financially speaking, was a serious one. The difficulty I see ahead will not be quite as severe, for the reason that in Canada we had some control. I hope this house will not applaud that statement too much, because that control was taken off by the powerful nation to the south before the control in Canada was removed. In the United States inflation reached a higher point than in this country; but from that inflation those charged with the responsibility of conducting affairs in that country were able to pad a cushion that will help them tide over the difficulty we are facing now; that is, not the collapse but the gradual recession in the prices of commodities.
Whilst controls were on, those of us in Canada who had the responsibility for the conduct of industry were not able to pile up that same cushion to take care of, not a depression but a decline in commodity prices. This decline in commodity prices is fast

Transitional Measures Act coming to our country in common with the United States. I hope it is a gradual decline and not precipitous. I hope the collapse, if I may use that expression for lack of a better one, or the gradual lowering of prices of all commodities, will not be too severe. When one considers this decline, I say that the lack of necessity for the ideas embodied in this particular resolution becomes more and more apparent. The need for the lessening of controls becomes more apparent because, with the lowering of commodity prices, in due course the law of supply and demand will take care of the necessity for having legislation such as this. I say to the government now, when it is framing the terms of the bill upon which this resolution is based: Do not incorporate in it anything which is not necessary. Let us get back to common sense, and let the law of supply and demand take care of the items which make it necessary for you to introduce this bill at this time.
I should like to mention, Mr. Speaker, one or two particular items. Perhaps I can be forgiven if they pertain to the community from which I come. The last items mentioned by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) were lumber and steel. I believe he will agree with me that the necessity for control of lumber is pretty well past. The control of lumber is not a large item, nowhere near as large as it was twenty-four months ago. You could almost forget about it. I feel that when the minister mentioned lumber he was sort of filling in. I leave it there.
In so far as steel is concerned, steel is in great demand. Steel undoubtedly requires some measure of regulation. For what reason? The reason is that projects of great magnitude, so far as this little country of Canada is concerned, have been held up for a great variety of reasons. To my mind, some of these reasons are patriotic. We had a war. We were told not to use steel while the war was on. We were told to forget, until the war was over, about our building projects requiring steel. The war consumed a tremendous amount of steel. Those charged with the responsibility for new construction requiring steel, realizing that a war requires a great quantity of this product, delayed their projects five years-yes, six, seven and eight years. The blueprints, however, were on the table. Those blueprints were worrying those who were directing the affairs of different organizations such as, for example, banks and office buildings.
May I give you a particular illustration in this regard? It is this that causes me to rise in my place tonight, and it concerns the necessary improvement of transportation in the city of Toronto which will require many


thousands of tons of steel. Hooking up that problem with the control of priorities, which is in the hands of the same minister, I ask the indulgence of this house to give consideration to that requirement of the city of Toronto. Including the metropolitan area, this city now has the tremendous population of a million people. In its handling of the transportation problem, it is ten or twenty years behind. Give the city of Toronto the steel required for this project which has already been delayed by one decade, if not close to two.
I urge this, Mr. Speaker, from the sensible and practical standpoint I mentioned a moment ago, that I was of the opinion that commodity prices are coming down. Let the bon. and sensible members of this house charged with the responsibility see to it that the commodity prices slide does not become a toboggan slide. Let them see to it that the bottom does not fall out of things as it did in 1922. I believe that the Minister of Trade and Commerce should give priority to the steel for that tremendous project in the city of Toronto which will help take a good deal of surplus steel off the market, and in the final analysis the Toronto taxpayers will not be in the position of having to pay more for the completion of their transportation system than they would have had to pay had there not been this control over the supply of steel. What I am trying to say is this: Let us soften the collapse of commodity prices by going ahead with projects of a kind that will not only absorb the production of steel, but will absorb that other and more important factor, the unemployed. During a period of recession in prices, the most important factor of all is keeping our people employed. Give the people the tools and materials to do the job so that employment will continue at a high level over this period which might become a transition period.
So far as other commodities are concerned, I say to the hon. members to my left not to worry too much about the cost of living. I can see a recession in commodity prices which will help that situation. Before I resume my seat, I should like to make one or two more suggestions in that regard.
I notice that at this moment the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) is in the chamber. As I look at him I think of the work he is doing on behalf of his department. I think of his $30 million expenditure spread over a period of years in a humanitarian cause. I hope that the minister of priorities, the minister of steel, will be generous to the Minister of National Health and Welfare when he approves of a scheme here and there which, in the final analysis, will relieve the suffering of humanity. When the Minister of National Health and Welfare spends his $13 million and finally his $30

million, and he finds projects delayed because of the minister of priorities and the minister of steel, I know, Mr. Speaker, that they will not even need to get together; a note from the Minister of National Health and Welfare to the minister of priorities will smooth the way so that these great projects to the credit of Canada and of the Department of National Health and Welfare, which are being undertaken in order that humanity may be served during sickness and for the preservation of the health of the whole community, will not run short of steel or lumber and may in due course go on with their construction.
I was addressing myself to some of the ideas that are running through the minds of some of the hon. members to my left. I was thinking of the high cost of living, and at the same time of rent control. I will try to describe the high cost of living as it appears to me, speaking on behalf of my constituency and myself. I am just as satisfied that the cost of living will not pyramid as I am of the fact that I am standing here, and that the cost of living will not go much higher. On the contrary, I am satisfied that it will come down. It will come down by using the efforts of our Canadian people to get more production not only for our own consumption but for export overseas. The overseas picture has not been too bright. I am not one of those who think it will get a great deal brighter with regard to our exports. Where will our exports find their port of destination? In days gone by they found it largely in the United Kingdom. Then it was a simple matter, because of the invisible balance of funds in the hands of the United Kingdom, which was our greatest customer, to take care of the requirement of getting Canadian dollars back into the hands and pockets of the producers of Canada. But that invisible balance which was so necessary in those days has fast disappeared. In the days to come, what is to take the place of that balance?
It has been my high privilege to observe what has happened to the world around. Although I am only an observer, I have some conception of the world financial situation. I think of the pound sterling versus the Canadian dollar and the American dollar. I think of Rhodesia producing tobacco the same as is produced in western Ontario. I think of Australia producing wheat and those great white-faced cattle they turn into beef for the British market. I think not only of products of that kind all down the line, but of products such as non-ferrous metals like zinc, lead, and so forth. Other parts of the world produce these commodities. We are in this spot. Those other parts of the world which produce these commodities I have men-
Transitional Measures Act tioned accept with gusto the British pound sterling as payment whereas they are unable to find Canadian dollars and American dollars, we will say, for the reason that they are unable to balance their trade payments. So to the other problems I have mentioned to a slight extent I add this additional problem: Whence will the 50,000,000 people of Britain receive their supplies or receive their food? The natural place from which these supplies will come is those countries in which they are produced and which are happy to accept the British pound sterling. So we must give some thought to that matter, having regard to the economy of Canada at this time. With that factor in the equation, I say to my hon. friends to my left: Do not cry too much about the high cost of living. World-wide factors and economic conditions will in turn take care of that problem, and we producers in this country of ours will be looking for consumers. When the law of supply and demand applies, in due course the cost of living will go down and find its proper level.
There is one other point to which I wish to refer before I resume my seat. Rent control has been a difficult problem and it has been difficult of administration. With so many people taking advantage of it, and so many people suffering from the lack of housing accommodation, a problem of the first magnitude is created for this honourable assembly. Many people are afraid to rent space they may have in their homes for fear that those who come in and occupy that space cannot be dispossessed in times when they are perhaps not behaving or in times when the immediate family which owns and operates the domestic establishment finds for one reason or another that it wants the space. What are the reasons, hon. members may ask. The answer is, the return from overseas, a few years ago, of young men bringing back English brides, and finding the upstairs flat of the father's home occupied by a tenant under rent control, as a result of which the son of the family and his new bride, and perhaps a youngster, were unable to get into the upstairs of the home, and live in peace and harmony with the father and mother. That is one reason.
The other reason is that there are selfish people who find themselves in a position of advantage, in that they happened to rent the premises during the period when rentals were depressed and wages were going up. On the one hand, the man and his wife accept the wages they receive, which were going up and up for two or three years, and at the same time refuse to pay their fair share of the cost of their lodgings, which cost was going up as far as the owner of the premises was

Transitional Measures Act concerned. Taxes were going up, and the cost of coal for heating purposes was going up, as was the general cost of the operation of a home. The owner found all those costs going up but not to the same degree the return from boarders or roomers, or from sublet premises. Those returns did not go up to the same extent. The net result is that there has been no peace and harmony among those people who have rented accommodation, and the owners have become so disgusted that, if they got these people out, never again would they rent premises to anyone whomsoever. I am of the opinion that when this rent control finally comes off, and these restrictions have been removed from the individuals who own premises and sublet them, there will be such an abundance of space offering, for those unfortunate enough not to have a domicile at the moment, that half of the difficulty of this problem will be solved. When the Minister of Finance rises in his place, as he did a few moments ago, and says that we will extend these controls of one kind and another to March 1950, I say to him: Give some thought to whether or not you mean March 1950, or whether you mean what the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) intimated-as soon as possible. Relieve the restrictions. Relieve the position. Help the position to cure itself. Do not dogmatically say March 1950. When we go into committee, tell this house that as long as you have in hand the administration of this particular feature of our controls, your officers will advise you. I do not hold the minister entirely responsible, Mr. Speaker. I do not like the word which has been used around here a good deal, but I cannot think of a better one. Perhaps the bureaucrats write the story for the minister. Perhaps the minister often tells the story as it is written. It is humanly impossible twenty-four hours a day for the minister to keep track of everything which is written and which he must be responsible for. He knows that as well as I do. I ask that ordinary common sense be the judge. I am just as sure as I stand here, in view of the predicament he is in now, in view of the predicament the country is in now, while many of these controls are being enforced, that if he uses common sense he will get rid of those portions of the controls which can be lifted without too much turmoil, which conditions will permit him to lift, and on lifting which public opinion will congratulate him. Do not do that all of a sudden in March 1950, but do it between now and then. He will not be there then; that is the difficulty. I say: Speed and oil up the machinery that is behind you. It does not need much oil; it seems to be well oiled. Increase the voltage a little bit and get rid of everything 

that public opinion wishes to be rid of, so that the shock and turmoil which will come in March 1950 will not be quite as severe as it looks as though it might be, looking at it from today's vantage point.
The Minister of Finance knows better than I do the commodities that are being subsidized. They have been an expensive luxury. They have been made necessary in his department by the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation which has gone into business. Government in business is not the best thing for a virile Canadian people. Government in business paying subsidies and stepping out into the market and of necessity buying commodities of one kind and another is not the best thing. You have had some experience of it, Mr. Speaker. When history is written, it will show on the credit side of the ledger some value to the Canadian people in so far as controls are concerned; but the government will not receive thanks for that value. On the other side of the ledger there will be a tremendous debit which has been added to the national debt, a national debt which will be bearing interest when my grandchildren and great-grandchildren are still wondering how democracy functioned during the days from 1945 to 1950. Therefore I say to the government: weigh these matters in the balance and get out of business. Get your Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation, backed by the wealth of Canada, out of business.
I can give a half dozen reasons why they should get out of business. The first one that runs through my mind, and the most potent of all, is this. Who are they to conduct this business on behalf of the government? They are the best men that the government could find. I admit that. They are honourable, upright and courageous. Many of them worked for $1 a year. But, Mr. Speaker, the war is over. Those who are left-and this is no reflection on them-are men who cannot find their way back into their own business. They know that the war is over. They know that in this particular vocation they are working on behalf of the government. They must realize in their quiet moments, when they are thinking over their life's work and their career, that they have served their country well. During the war they served to their own disadvantage. Financially speaking, perhaps, they might have gone farther ahead if they had stuck to their own business. Now that the war is over, let them get back to the vocations for which they were trained and apprenticed. Let them do that in our behalf and in behalf of private enterprise. Let us get out of business as far as government is concerned.

The thought runs through my mind, as I think about the career of many of these great Canadians who have been of such service to the government during the tragic days of the war, that they have aged since then. Five years in these positions means ten years. It is most unfortunate if, during their declining days, or during the days when they have not the push and initiative that they had when the war first broke out, they have to be kept in positions sponsored, and paid for, by this government. That is a sad thing for Canada. 1 say that the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation, mentioned by the minister when he spoke of flour-

Let us in an orderly businesslike way, to the general weal of the whole of Canada, get rid of the necessity of having these control organizations. At the same time I add a word of caution. Be careful that you assume your full responsibility with regard to any organization, whatever it may be, which in any way may form a cartel or gang up on any particular commodity to the disadvantage of Canada. Transitional Measures Act price control and let Canadians know that that act is to be enforced, and in the final analysis I am of the opinion that the Canadian people will be glad to be rid of these controls which put the government in business. Do that as soon as is reasonably possible. I did not say get rid of all controls. Avoid the shock of March, 1950-and meantime probably we will be over there to do it for you.
I say to the government, take some of the power now behind controls and put it behind the act which protects our Canadian people from monopolies and cartels. If that were done, this country would ultimately be far better off.
